items.text:
Wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi encountered the shot of a lifetime in Damaraland, Namibia. In September 2025, he witnessed a desert elephant carrying its stillborn calf. What resulted was an arresting black-and-white image that is beautifully composed but ultimately full of grief. The close-up portrait shows the mother with her deceased calf between her tusk and trunk, as if she is unable to let her baby go. The emotional image, titled The Aftermath , was recognized in the prestigious Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 competition , with Veronesi earning the title of Overall Winner and the Behavior Mammals category winner.
Veronesi was tracking elephants when he noticed an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed. He understood why when he saw the mother and child. “The calf’s body rose up and in this particular frame, it almost looks like the calf is still alive, playing with its mother or trying to cling to her mother’s trunk,” he recalls to My Modern Met. “I feel that the ambiguity of the image, and how it can be read in many ways make it stand out from the other images I took, where the calf is clearly hanging lifeless from the mother’s tusk.”
The photographer initially felt conflicted about capturing the scene. “After taking the first few images, I felt like I was violating the elephant’s intimate moment, her grief, I was almost ashamed and thought that I shouldn’t take these photographs,” he shares. But ultimately, Veronesi found it important to highlight the complexity of these creatures. Elephants have been observed engaging in behaviors around death, including vocalizing, guarding the deceased, and carrying the dead, as pictured. By photographing this painful moment, Veronesi shows us that wildlife and humans aren’t as far apart as we may think.
We spoke with Veronesi about capturing the poignant shot, his philosophy about photographing wildlife, and more. Scroll down for My Modern Met’s exclusive interview.
What is your photography background, and how did you begin photographing wildlife?
Photography was part of my life since an early age as I grew up in a family of keen nature photographers. Every travel or outing was always centered on photographing nature, birds and wildlife in particular. I therefore learned photography almost naturally. items.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
items.desc: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
items.text:
SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.
Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

items.title: Delia Smith joins opponents of £1.2bn data centre
items.desc: The TV cook and author is worried about the environmental impact of the proposed Keswick facility.
items.text:
Watch: Delia Smith says data centre will be bad for county
Television cook Delia Smith has joined opponents of a £1.2bn data centre, arguing it would threaten a nature reserve.
Campaigners fear the proposed centre at Keswick, on the edge of Norwich, will create noise pollution and have a negative impact on nearby Marston Marsh.
Smith, honorary life president and former majority shareholder of Norwich City FC, said: "I love Norfolk. You can't be involved in a football club for 55 years without being attached to the people and the beauty of Norfolk. I feel very strongly about it."
But developer Norwich Apex said an ecological impact assessment concluded no effect on the reserve was expected.
Delia Smith, pictured with fellow campaigner Jake Humphrey, says she feels very strongly about protecting Norfolk
Data centres are facilities that store and process vast amounts of data and run the software and online services used by millions of people.
This centre, off the A140 Ipswich Road, would need 150 MW of power to run and would feature 72 chiller units on its roof.
According to planning documents, the building would be about 20m (65ft) high.
A planning application for the centre has been lodged with South Norfolk Council.
If approved, construction could begin at the end of 2027 and it would be operational by 2028.
The plans have emerged at the same time as a much bigger proposal for a data centre and solar farm elsewhere in Norfolk, south of King's Lynn, which would require more than five times as much electricity.
What are data centres and are more coming to the East?
The developer has said the Keswick facility would use " air-cooling technology " and not require water for cooling.
But Smith, who lives in Suffolk, said: "We haven't got enough water, and data centres use an awful lot of water.
""It's one of the biggest [data centres] and It doesn't do anything for the Norfolk community. Where is the £1.2bn coming from? And who are the people who are going to presumably make money out of it?
"It's not going to do anything for the local community, it's the opposite. It's going to be bad."
Campaigners have raised concerns about the proposed centre's effect on the nearby Marston Marsh nature reserve
It is hoped the centre will harness wind energy by connecting to the Hornsea 3 substation nearby.
Smith said: "Renewable energy is going into the grid but it doesn't supply everything now.

items.title: “Nobody Knew It Was Here”: 47 Fun Facts That Might Surprise Even The Most Curious Minds
items.desc: Curiosity can send us down internet rabbit holes and sometimes leave us in a 2 am Wikipedia vortex just to scratch a random brain itch. But you don’t have to do all that heavy lifting today — we’ve rounded up some of the most fascinating facts and mind-blowing stories about humans, science, nature, history, and everyday life — all packed into one easy-to-read list right here. So dive in to learn s
items.text:
Space discoveries, inventions, historical tales, and everyday news stories might seem like totally separate topics. Yet they all share the same root: our drive to explore the unknown and understand our place in the world.
People aren’t always trying to build the next big gadget right out of the gate, yet this basic urge to find answers drives our greatest tools and inventions.
For example, consider how penicillin was discovered. Scientist Alexander Fleming wasn’t trying to save millions of lives or win a prize when he went to work that day. He just spotted some weird mold growing in a messy dish and wondered what it was. That one spark of wonder changed modern medicine forever.
You don’t need a lab coat to enjoy the perks of an active mind. Looking up random trivia and digging into strange tales can actually change how your brain works in daily life.
Research shows that when something grabs our interest, the reward centers in our heads light up and release dopamine. Even though a fun fact isn’t a physical treat like cold water or a sweet snack, our minds still react to it like a prize. We are built to feel good when we learn something new.
The rush of feel-good chemicals when we learn something new can also make our memory sharper.
In 2014 , neuroscientist Charan Ranganath and his team at the University of California, Davis, tested how this works by scanning people’s brains while they answered trivia questions. They found that curiosity peaks when we know a little about a subject, only to realize a piece of the puzzle is missing. That gap creates a strong pull to find the answer.
“When we compare trials where people are highly curious to know an answer with trials where they are not, and look at the differences in brain activity, it beautifully follows the pathways in the brain that are involved in transmitting dopamine signals,” said Dr. Ranganath. “The activity ramps up, and the amount it ramps up is highly correlated with how curious they are."
During experiments, the University of California researchers noticed something else amazing. Whenever a person really wanted an answer, their hippocampus — the brain's main memory center of the brain — woke up alongside the reward system.
This burst of energy helped them recall the trivia later, and also remember random details shown in between, like strangers’ faces. Once curiosity kicks in, your mind turns into a giant sponge that soaks up all kinds of details around you.

items.title: Huge fly-tip grew undetected over several months
items.desc: The council says the 20-tonne pile of rubbish was dumped over garden fences.
items.text:
The waste was dumped over garden fences in South Wigston over several months
Two fly-tippers were able to dump huge amounts of household waste over their garden fences without being detected for several months, with the pile eventually reaching 20 tonnes.
It was spotted on land owned by a business in South Wigston, Leicestershire, earlier in the year.
However, due to the location of the fly-tip, it was not immediately visible to employees of the business, which Oadby and Wigston Borough Council said "allowed the offenders to act over several months".
The two individuals responsible were each issued with a £600 fixed penalty notice following an interview under caution, the authority added, while a third person was cautioned for their role in the offence.
Before the rubbish could be cleared, the council's environmental health officers worked with the business to gather evidence to prove who had been responsible.
The authority has not specified which business was affected by the fly-tipping, or from where the rubbish was sourced.
The waste was reported to Oadby and Wigston Borough Council
The council said it had also recently issued another £600 fine after a resident's waste was found in a lay-by off Gartree Road in Oadby.
They had not fly-tipped the rubbish themselves, the authority added, but had paid a rogue operator in good faith to take it away.
According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.
Councillor Samina Haq, leader of the council, said: "There is simply no excuse for fly-tipping. It damages our environment, costs money to clear up and is unfair on the overwhelming majority of residents and businesses who dispose of their waste responsibly.
"These successful cases send a clear message that we will investigate reports, gather evidence and take action against those responsible.
"Please continue to report fly-tipping whenever you see it and, if you pay someone to remove your waste, always make sure they are properly licensed."

items.desc: While a little boy was fighting a deadly disease in the Children’s Hospital of New Orleans he longed for a place to go get some fresh air or distraction from his woes. Before he died, he and his family started a foundation to raise money—and five years later his wish was fulfilled. items.text:
While a little boy was fighting a deadly disease in the Children’s Hospital of New Orleans he longed for a place to go get some fresh air or distraction from his woes. Before he died, he and his family started a foundation to raise money—and five years later his wish was fulfilled.
Last week, his family celebrated the opening of the world’s first museum incorporated into a hospital—a fantastical ‘Imaginarium’ where sick kids and their families can go for art, movement, pretending, and fun.
Named after the nine-year-old, Walker Beery, Walker’s Imaginarium is a 15,000-square-foot children’s museum where patients can wander through rooms interacting with uniquely Louisiana themes: dancing to cajun music, exploring a bayou, joining a Mardi Gras parade, or enjoying a quiet moment among an animated fish tank.
Designed for a range of physical, sensory, and medical needs, kids in wheelchairs can play both mini-golf and foosball while rolling by the colorful ramps and murals—and forgetting they’re in a hospital. (See the video at the bottom…)
For the Beery family, Walker’s Imaginarium is a deeply personal expression of their son Walker’s vision to give back to others. In August 2019, he was diagnosed with pediatric brain cancer, yet through surgeries, hospital stays, and chemotherapy treatments, Walker’s infectious courage and grateful spirit always amazed his family and all who encountered him during his two-year battle at the hospital, recently renamed Manning Family Children’s.
Walker’s Imaginarium was funded entirely through philanthropic support and donations raised by the community and the lad’s foundation, Kids Join The Fight .
“Walker’s spirit is carried forward in the joy that is embedded in this amazing project,” said Walker’s dad Taylor, co-founder of Kids Join The Fight.
“Every child who finds a moment of escape, every family that experiences joy together carries Walker’s dream forward: to use his own experience to make someone else’s a little easier, and a little happier.”
Designed around the needs of young patients, the interactive experiences use therapeutic play to relieve the burden of long hospitalizations and support holistic recovery.
By integrating feedback from clinical experts and patient families, the design team transformed health challenges into opportunities for play-based healing.
From the very first step into Walker’s Imaginarium, visitors are invited to create their own dance party, complete with interactive lights, marching band music

items.title: One-of-a-Kind Refuge to 200,000 Walrus Protected Forever in Alaska
items.desc: American conservationists have secured protections for a truly unique-in-the-world ecosystem along the state’s Bering Sea coastline. Home to the largest concentrations of Pacific walrus found anywhere in North America, the barrier islands off the coast of the tiny northern village of Point Lay provide a critical refuge for these marine megafauna. Now ensconced within a […] The post One-of-a-Kind R
items.text:
American conservationists have secured protections for a truly unique-in-the-world ecosystem along the state’s Bering Sea coastline.
Home to the largest concentrations of Pacific walrus found anywhere in North America, the barrier islands off the coast of the tiny northern village of Point Lay provide a critical refuge for these marine megafauna.
Now ensconced within a 47,000-acre protected area (74 square miles) held by the Interior Alaska Land Trust, the islands have been spared from industrial development and other disturbances, as has “one of the largest, undiminished coastal lagoon systems in the world,” which was protected in tandem.
Part of the coalition that for 10 years has worked towards securing protections for the Point Lay barrier islands and the Kasegaluk Lagoon, The Conservation Fund explains that the islands hadn’t historically been a walrus mecca until 2007, when the animals changed their seasonal migration behavior in mass.
Every year, a quarter million Pacific walrus would migrate north through the Bering Strait, with the males remaining out at sea and the females with their calves moving towards the shallow, nutrient-rich waters of the Chukchi Sea between Alaska and Russia.
Historically, these animals relied on Arctic sea ice for resting spots, but by 2007 the ice had become inconsistent. One year, an estimated 200,000 walrus hauled themselves up onto the barrier islands of Point Lay, and they’ve returned every year ever since.
That includes every single female and juvenile Pacific walrus on Earth—all stuffed onto beaches that will now forever be theirs thanks to The Conservation Fund and its partners among the Alaska tribal nations and the Interior Alaska Land Trust.
The new conservation easement was bought by the Fund from an Alaska Native Corporation the Cully Corp. It will be held by the Trust, which will increase monitoring and stewardship to actively minimize disturbance to walrus and other animals as commercial and tourist activity in the Alaskan Arctic continues to expand. Conservation Fund noted that encroachment from humans had already caused undesirable stampede events among the resting animals.

items.title: More Than 50 Dancers Will Celebrate Our Connection to the Ocean During Miami Art Week
items.desc: More Than 50 Dancers Will Celebrate Our Connection to the Ocean During Miami Art Week As part of Miami Art Week, more than 50 dancers and members of the public will come together on Miami Beach to celebrate our deep and lasting relationship with the sea. The Ocean Odyssey is a new, site-specific performance by Indian artist Subodh Kerkar, presented in partnership with the Andaz Miami Beach Resort
items.text:
As part of Miami Art Week, more than 50 dancers and members of the public will come together on Miami Beach to celebrate our deep and lasting relationship with the sea. The Ocean Odyssey is a new, site-specific performance by Indian artist Subodh Kerkar , presented in partnership with the Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa , the Miami City Ballet , and its artistic director, Gonzalo García.
Kerkar describes the ocean as “a symbol of celebration of one humanity,” adding, “I celebrate the inseparability of human life and the ocean.” The artist is inviting up to 60 members of the public to join professional dancers in the performance. Together, they’ll move across the beach in a carefully choreographed sequence, creating lines and shapes—like straight lines, wavy lines, and circle formations—that are particularly striking when viewed from above. As Kerkar explains , “No dance experience needed: it begins as a simple walk, and from above, it becomes something extraordinary.”
The Ocean Odyssey will take place on Dec. 4, between 4-5 p.m., in front of Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa. It’s organized by REEFLINE , a non-profit and pioneering underwater public sculpture park at Miami Beach. REEFLINE is creating a new kind of underwater reef, bringing together art, science, and technology to support marine restoration, encourage biodiversity, and help ocean ecosystems thrive.

The former […] The post Retired Teacher Turns Retired Musical Instruments into Bird Feeders (LOOK) appeared
items.text:
A Canadian man is writing a coda into the lives of scrapped musical instruments by using them to offer a free lunch to his feathered neighbors.
A nibble of corn or seed comes with no strings attached at the Frets and Feathers Cafe, run by retired teacher Rob Burke from Prince Edward Island.
The former math teacher saw someone from Europe make an old guitar into a birdfeeder on social media and figured he could do one better: a three-course orchestra.
Asking for donations of broken instruments for an art project on Facebook, Burke was delighted to receive 6 guitars, an old violin, and pieces of a drum set.
He got to work attaching driftwood perches and metal feeding dishes into the hollow-body guitars.
CBC reported that his choice of a glue gun was just fine at first, but once the heavier blue jays began visiting, he had to reattach the perches and dishes more firmly.
His Facebook wall features an array of common birds, which Burke says he has taken a greater interest in since retiring. Videos are often paired with music, and make for great viewing.
He has since seen a woodpecker, corvids, and chickadees, and expects to see further species as the seasons change.
For any other PE Islanders, Burke welcomes further instrument donations to expand the Peck and Play Orchestra. One can contact him over Facebook.

items.title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
items.desc: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.
items.text:
As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.

items.title: Roman Glass Among the Silk Road Treasures Unearthed in Nomadic Noble’s Tomb
items.desc: The legendary character of the Silk Road was in full focus recently in Mongolia, where excavations of a nomad’s tomb unearthed objects all the way from Classical Rome. The tomb undoubtedly belonged to an elite individual from the Xiongnu people, a nomadic group that controlled large stretches of Central Asia, Mongolia, and Manchuria for some […] The post Roman Glass Among the Silk Road Treasures U
items.text:
The legendary character of the Silk Road was in full focus recently in Mongolia, where excavations of a nomad’s tomb unearthed objects all the way from Classical Rome.
The tomb undoubtedly belonged to an elite individual from the Xiongnu people, a nomadic group that controlled large stretches of Central Asia, Mongolia, and Manchuria for some 5 centuries.
In addition to a cup made from Roman glass, a gourd-shaped silver and crystal pendant, likely used to adorn a horse’s harness, closely resembles accessories found in tombs on the Korean Peninsula that date to the same period.
The discoveries highlight the Xiongnu’s role in a vast exchange network that linked these progenitors of the conquering Mongols to the Roman Empire, Han China, and the Korean Peninsula.
The Xiongnu’s role in East Asian history cannot be overstated, as much for what these nomadic horse archers did themselves as for what they brought out of their southern neighbors, the Han Chinese. To face down these ferocious warriors, the Chinese stamped their names into the history books with the building of the first Great Wall of China.
A need to secure horses to wage war on the Xiongnu required a stable route to Central Asia, which saw the establishment of Chinese control over the Gansu Corridor. This paved the way for the first iteration of the Silk Road out across the deserts and steppes of the Tarim Basin through to Modern-day Uzbekistan.
The Xiongnu existed as the most powerful confederation of nomadic tribes on the steppe for almost 5 centuries, a span of control unmatched until the rise of Genghis Khan over 1,000 years after their ultimate defeat by the Han.
Located in the Duurlig Nars burial ground, which contains around 300 graves, the newly excavated Tomb 160 is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia to date. The exterior measures nearly 240 feet in length, but the interior chamber is surprisingly small and shallow, extending only about 50 feet deep.
This contrasts with deeper tombs in central Mongolia, suggesting changes in Xiongnu society during the late first and second centuries CE, a period when the empire was declining due to internal conflicts and pressure from the Han military.

items.title: ‘Extraordinary’ Drug May Actually Cure High Blood Pressure Caused by Hormones, And it’s FDA-Approved
items.desc: Millions of people with high blood pressure may be offered an actual cure for its root cause that would bring long-lasting relief. Doctors were stunned by the latest study of patients who took the FDA-approved drug called baxdrostat, which showed that it reversed the condition—even for years after patients stopped taking the medication. Baxdrostat (aka […] The post ‘Extraordinary’ Drug May Actuall
items.text:
Millions of people with high blood pressure may be offered an actual cure for its root cause that would bring long-lasting relief.
Doctors were stunned by the latest study of patients who took the FDA-approved drug called baxdrostat, which showed that it reversed the condition—even for years after patients stopped taking the medication.
Baxdrostat (aka Baxfendy) is the first of a specific type of medication, known as extended aldosterone synthase inhibition (EASI), to hit the US market—although there are others, like lorundrostat, in the pipeline.
“Just under a quarter of the patients came off all treatment and had completely normal blood pressure,” Prof. Morris Brown, a hypertension specialist who led the study at Queen Mary University of London told The Guardian .
The treatment involves taking the new class of drugs for 6-12 months to target excess production of the hormone aldosterone, a common cause of high blood pressure. Unlike conventional treatments that control blood pressure, the EASI-treatment appears to reverse its underlying cause, removing the need for lifelong medication.
The findings raise the possibility that, for people with this type of high blood pressure—between 5 and 10% of hypertension cases—a cure is possible.
Previously, if your adrenal glands were producing too much aldosterone, it caused the kidneys to retain excess salt, raising your blood pressure—and the only cure was surgery to remove the entire gland.
The study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, followed 14 people treated at eight centers across the US. Researchers found that the EASI-treatment led to sustained reversal of excess aldosterone production and partial or complete resolution of high blood pressure for up to two years after treatment ended.
Hormone levels and blood pressure remained similar to, or lower than, those recorded during their treatment, suggesting that the benefits could persist long after people stop taking the drug.
The scientific basis for EASI-treatment dates back to a 2005 experiment in mice, which showed that deleting the gene responsible for producing aldosterone synthase caused the cells that make aldosterone to disappear. Researchers at Queen Mary predicted that prolonged treatment with an aldosterone synthase inhibitor might have a similar effect in humans, potentially removing the underlying cause of their hypertension.

items.title: Good News in History, November 24
items.desc: 167 years ago today, the British naturalist and geologist Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species explaining his theory of evolution. The first edition—which has been voted by publishers and librarians as the most influential academic book ever written—introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of […] The post Good News in Hi
items.text:
167 years ago today, the British naturalist and geologist Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species explaining his theory of evolution. The first edition—which has been voted by publishers and librarians as the most influential academic book ever written—introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of natural selection. It presented a body of evidence that the diversity of life arose by common descent through a tree-like branching pattern of evolution. WATCH an animation about how little finches were crucial to his discovery, and how pepper moths evolved due to pollution… (1859)
Darwin included evidence that he had gathered on expeditions to South America in the 1830s and his subsequent findings from research and experimentation, and showed how natural selection is a scientifically testable mechanism. Within two decades widespread scientific agreement solidified that evolution had occurred, and by the mid-20th century Darwin’s concept of evolutionary adaptation through natural selection became central to modern evolutionary theory—and the unifying concept of the life sciences.
Modern evolutionary theory continues to develop, but his writings still explain the diversity of living organisms and their adaptation to the environment; make sense of the geological record; and hold up under modern genome analysis.
Because of church teachings at the time, his theory was much maligned, but clergymen later came to accept natural selection, explaining it as an instrument of God’s design. The Vatican stated its official position in 1950, which held that evolution was consistent with Catholic teachings. Darwin, himself, believed at the outset that God had been creating life through the laws of nature.

items.title: 68 Thanksgiving Memes That Sum Up The Food, Family, And Festive Frustrations
items.desc: Thanksgiving is supposed to be about gratitude, family, and enjoying a delicious meal, but the holiday comes with plenty of chaos, too. From relatives asking awkward questions and hosts struggling to prepare an enormous feast to guests eating until they can barely move, there's no shortage of moments worth laughing about. Add in the pressure of making everything perfect, and it's easy to see why T
items.text:
Thanksgiving is one of the most recognizable holidays in the United States, but its history stretches much further back than the familiar family feast suggests. According to the BBC , the holiday originated from harvest celebrations and religious days of giving thanks that existed long before the United States adopted it as an annual tradition.
Although the story most commonly associated with Thanksgiving centers on a 1621 harvest feast in Plymouth, Massachusetts, European settlers had already organized similar celebrations in North America. One documented religious service took place in Newfoundland in 1578, while Spanish settlers in Florida may have held earlier gatherings.
Initially, these occasions were generally solemn religious observances rather than the elaborate family celebrations people recognize today.
Over the following centuries, Thanksgiving gradually developed into a more established holiday. In 1789, President George Washington proclaimed November 26 a national day of public thanksgiving and prayer, although it would take much longer for the familiar traditions to take shape.
The modern Thanksgiving menu, including turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, and pumpkin pie, developed gradually rather than being a direct recreation of the 1621 feast. During the 20th century , large family dinners, parades, and football games became increasingly important parts of the celebration.
Today, Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November and is often associated with bringing loved ones together, although its colonial history and connections to Indigenous communities remain important parts of the holiday's story.
Over time, the holiday has accumulated plenty of customs that make it recognizable to millions of Americans. National Geographic explains that Thanksgiving traditionally revolves around a shared meal, expressions of gratitude, and spending time with family and friends.
Turkey usually takes center stage, accompanied by familiar dishes such as stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy, sweet potatoes, cranberry sauce, and pumpkin or pecan pie. Many households also begin dinner with a prayer or take turns sharing what they are thankful for.
Beyond the dinner table, the holiday has become associated with public celebrations, particularly the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, which first took place in New York City in 1924. Football has also become a major part of the occasion, with the NFL making Thanksgiving games a regular tradition in 1934.

items.text:
A major success in population-scale control of mosquito-borne viruses comes now from Brazil, where schoolchildren are enjoying a 68% lower risk of such diseases.
The trial tested the largely-proven method of releasing mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria, which inhibits the insect’s ability to spread viruses like dengue, Zika, and chikungunya.
Trialed over 4 years in Belo Horizonte, the success overlapped with the largest outbreak of dengue fever ever recorded in Brazil, demonstrating the urgent need for greater mosquito control in the tropics.
“The intervention substantially reduced dengue infections during Brazil’s largest recorded outbreak, demonstrating its potential to protect communities even under conditions of intense transmission,” states Derek Cummings, PhD, co-principal investigator of the trial and Bloomberg Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins University, one of the institutions that participated.
Called the EVITA dengue trial, the international team set out to test a locally-adapted version of the wMel strain of Wolbachia for use in inhibiting viral transmission from Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
wMel is the most commonly-used strain of Wolbachia, with the ‘Mel’ referring to the fruit fly species from which Wolbachia was first isolated. wMel-infected mosquitoes pass the bacteria to their offspring, thereby inhibiting disease transmission on a generational scale.
EVITA included 58 school-defined geographic clusters in Belo Horizonte, with 29 clusters assigned to receive releases of wMel mosquitoes in addition to standard vector-control measures, and 29 clusters assigned to standard vector control alone, such as insecticidal sprays and mosquito source reduction.
The randomized-controlled trial released Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes from January 2021 through May 2022. It involved 5,757 school children, ages 6 to 11. The results were presented on Saturday at the American Society of Tropical Medicine & Hygiene annual meeting in National Harbor, Maryland.

items.text:
Once a year, the owners of a Texas auto-repair shop would refurbish a donated car and then hand the keys to a member of their community in need.
But thanks to their generosity and the generosity of others, they’ve been able to turbocharge their giving, with multiple vehicles going out ever year.
“One was not enough,” says wife Cathy Bailey. “Once we experienced it, you want more,” adds husband Dane.
Indeed, giving away cars is their joy of joys, and something that thanks to their Colleyville community, they can now do multiple times per year.
Autos for Love started years ago when the Baileys, who own Auto Experts of Colleyville , wanted to try and put in a little more elbow grease on behalf of those who have no wheels to grease.
Refurbishing gently used cars donated by community members, their aim was to give away one per year. But seeing the reaction of the recipients quickly pushed them to try and find more cars, and more people in need.
Reported on first by WFAA News , Autos for Love attracted a lot of attention, and soon became turbo-charged with donated vehicles.
This year, the Baileys began looking for who in town needed them the most, and some residents called in to nominate their friend Barbara Farison, a mother whose car was totaled by another motorist running a red light.
Unable to secure a replacement, Farison and her kids have walked everywhere for 3 years when alternative transportation wasn’t available, including to school and to buy groceries. It has exposed them to toil, the elements, and in Farison’s case, to an incident of violent crime she only narrowly avoided.
When her friends got wind of Autos for Love, they called up the Baileys to explain the situation, who then in turn called Farison and invited her to the shop, ostensibly for an “interview.”
Instead, she suddenly found her palms filled with the keys to a 2005 Acura MDX.
“This is the biggest blessing,” Farison said. “I cannot explain to you how much easier this is going to be for my kids and myself. It’s going to make my mommy heart extremely happy.”
Farison was one of 4 people who received cars from the Baileys that day, meaning that this year alone they have given away 8 autos with love.

items.title: 65 Times Americans Thought They Lived In The Only Country In The World
items.desc: The internet has made it easier than ever to learn about the world, but apparently, not everyone feels the need to take advantage of that. Some online discussions quickly turn into reminders that the United States isn't the only country on the map. From confusing international currencies to assuming everyone follows American time zones, these posts capture some wonderfully baffling examples of geo
items.text:
Call it US defaultism, the quiet assumption that the United States is the default setting for every topic. Ask about the legal drinking age, school holidays or the cost of a hospital visit, and someone will answer as though only one country exists. Most of the time there is no bad intent behind it. People simply never had to notice the frame around their own view, a bit like a fish who has never been introduced to the concept of water.
Part of the answer is plain geography. The country is enormous, with Texas alone covering more ground than France, and you can drive for days without seeing a border. Two oceans guard the coasts, and the only land neighbors are Canada and Mexico.
Compare that with Europe, where a weekend trip can mean a new language over breakfast. Americans do travel, of course, but USAFacts puts the number of valid passports at roughly 48 for every 100 people, and that count even includes folks who hold both a passport book and a card. Plenty of people simply never had a reason to get one.
Language plays a big role too. A Pew Research Center analysis found that a median of 92% of European students study a foreign language in school, compared with about 20% of students across the American school system. A newer Pew report from 2026 adds that only 43% of public schools in the US offer world language classes at all, even though most adults say children should learn one.
Attitudes differ by location, with 52% of urban adults calling language learning important compared with 28% of rural adults. Then there is the internet, where W3Techs estimates that English is used by about half of all websites whose language it can identify. An American can scroll for hours without ever feeling like a visitor.
Never miss a story that brings joy to the world. Add us on Google
The classroom adds to the picture. In the 2018 edition of the Nation's Report Card , only about 25% of eighth graders reached the proficient level in geography. That is a demanding bar, to be fair, but it still leaves plenty of room for confusion. When the map of the world arrives as an afterthought, it is hardly shocking that a confident comment about Georgia ends up pointing at Atlanta.
The classic proof comes from a National Geographic and Roper survey of young Americans aged 18 to 24, conducted in 2006 . Bayless is best known perhaps for a docu-series he made with PBS called Mexico: One Plate at a Time.

items.desc: More than 400 years after the Pilgrims first explored the Cape Cod area, land belonging to Native Americans was returned to Indigenous ownership. items.text:
More than 400 years after the Pilgrims first explored the Cape Cod area, land belonging to Native Americans was returned to Indigenous ownership.
On October 30, The Nature Conservancy gave roughly 126 acres of salt marsh and natural habitat in Eastham, Massachusetts to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit based in Mashpee. The land sits right next to a 20.4-acre parcel the Conservancy bought earlier in the year for $3 million, linking them into a larger protected area that looks out over First Encounter Beach. ⁠
“This place holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed,” Ramona Peters, founder and board president of the Native Land Conservancy and a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, said in a published statement . “Long before the first encounter, Native people lived here and took care of this land.”
In December 1620, not long after the Mayflower arrived, an exploring party led by Myles Standish traded arrows and gunfire with Nauset warriors near what’s now called First Encounter Beach, named for the first hostile meeting between the Pilgrims and a native people.
The fight came after colonists had taken corn and disturbed graves. “Our ancestors weren’t just standing around. They were protecting their families, and taking care of this land lets us tell that story the right way,” R. Peters said.
The First Encounter with the Nauset on Cape Cod happened before the better-known harvest feast with the Wampanoag at Plymouth in 1621, but even that meeting lacked context. The Wampanoag were never invited; 90 warriors arrived and were invited to stay as an act of diplomacy after responding to celebratory musket fire from the colonists.
“The Thanksgiving holiday overlooks a myriad of sins. The backstory to colonization includes enslavement of Native men, the introduction of a devastating plague, the theft of corn and disturbance of graves of the Nauset people, and an alliance that robed the Wampanoag of their sovereignty and land,” Paula Peters, communications and program director at the Native Land Conservancy, said.
The salt marsh and nearby uplands also give a home to vulnerable animals, including diamondback terrapins that nest along the coastal bluffs. The 20.4-acre property next door—bought in June 2026 with help from the Eastham Conservation Foundation and local neighbors—has been named T8nupâhs Uwatuhshât, which means “at the turtle’s nest” in the Wôpanâak language.

A new thumb implant is transforming hand function for people with advanced arthritis.
Traditionally, doctors remove the trapezium, a small bone at the thumb’s base
To overcome “bone-on-bone contact” the new treatment that uses a “ball-and-socket” designed as an insert for repairing the trapezium.
In trials, patients who received the thumb implants gained a range of motion—and it stayed stronger over the long term.
Thumb arthritis (carpometacarpal osteoarthritis) is a debilitating condition that effects millions of Americans and can dramatically impact hand use and daily quality of life.
Performed more than 130,000 times in Europe since gaining approval there, its use is now spreading across the United States after receiving FDA approval last year.
The Swiss-designed CMC Touch 1 prosthesis, developed and manufactured by KeriMedical, does not require any anatomy changes. Surgeons use the same approach they are already familiar with—like a mini hip replacement for the thumb.
“The mechanics of it are a ball and socket joint to replace the saddle joint that is your thumb,” said orthopedic surgeon Dr. Stephen Berling, who was trained in the procedure in Ohio.
Traditional thumb reconstruction is used when bone-on-bone arthritis occurs where the thumb meets the wrist. The procedure involves removing the trapezium bone and then resuspending the thumb, but there are big downsides.
The thumb may take time to function properly without the bone, requiring a lengthy recovery of six to nine months, with patients in a splint or cast for 6 weeks.
On the other hand, recent patients who’ve receive the TOUCH prosthesis, which helps restore pinch and grip strength, are leaving the operating room with just an ACE bandage.
With this new implant, the bone is not removed, which provides immediate stability and helps accelerate recovery. The outpatient surgery takes about 45 minutes, allows patients to go home the same day. (Stitches stay in for two weeks, and once they are removed, patients can shower and get their hand wet.)

items.desc: Strong winds and heavy rain are expected to impact celebrations across the USA, with the risk that the famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade could be impacted.
items.text:
The sun shone on 2025's Thanksgiving Parade but the forecast this year is not so bright
Strong winds are threatening to disrupt Thursday's Thanksgiving parade in New York City for the first time since World War Two.
A potent Nor'easter storm could impact the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade which is due to be taking place for the 100th time, with the risk that it could be too windy for the event's iconic balloons to fly.
The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade is due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern USA as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow.
Western areas of the country have also faced Thanksgiving travel headaches, with Pacific storms and coastal flooding.
Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions
The parade started life as the Macy's Christmas Parade, organised by employees at Macy's department store in New York City in a bid to boost holiday sales.
The first event took place on Thanksgiving Day 1924. It has only been cancelled during World War Two, when it was put on hiatus between 1942 and 1944. As a result, this year marks the 100th parade.
It is due to take place from 08:30 local time (13:30 GMT), ending at around 12:00 (17:00 GMT) , and involves marching bands, street performers and floats parading through the streets of New York City, as well as 100 brightly-coloured inflatable balloons.
Confetti filled the air above this enormous turkey at the start of the 2025 parade
However, due to city regulations full-size balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23mph (37km/h), or in gusts of more than 35mph (56km/h).
There is a risk that Thursday will bring winds approaching those strengths.
However, record wind gusts also made the 1997 route a no-fly zone and the balloons were still featured in the parade.
The giant character balloons were tethered to golf carts that year.
In 1989, when a major snowstorm stopped balloon handlers getting to the parade route, the cheer and dance teams stepped in to pull the giant balloons along.

items.title: 59 Amazing Things About Humanity To Remind You There Is Still Hope
items.desc: Humans are capable of some truly incredible things, and sometimes all it takes is one moment to remind us of that. From mind-blowing talents and brilliant ideas to extraordinary feats that seem almost impossible, people never stop finding new ways to amaze us. Here are some of the most impressive examples of humans being absolutely awesome.
items.text:
What makes someone exceptionally good at something? Being highly skilled takes much more than just natural talent. People who excel in areas like music, sports, chess, or medicine usually spend years improving specific skills. Their success comes from lots of practice and making changes that help them handle tougher challenges.
Skilled performers also learn special ways to process information. For example, chess players spot patterns that help them guess what might happen next, while other experts build memory skills to handle complex information better. These abilities let them make decisions and react more quickly.
Practice is especially helpful when people get good feedback and use it to fix their mistakes. Instead of just repeating the same things, skilled performers keep changing how they work and focus on their weak spots. Over time, this helps them get better and do things they once thought were impossible.
But what makes someone want to try new things and build new skills in the first place? Curiosity is a big part of it. People who like to explore new topics, try out ideas, and learn new things often show more creativity. Wanting to see what happens next can be the first step toward something amazing.
There’s an interesting link between curiosity and creativity. People who look for new experiences and information are more likely to think creatively than those who just want to solve a problem. In other words, exploring just because something is interesting can really help creativity.
Curiosity also encourages people to look for new solutions. Instead of thinking something has to work a certain way, they might try different methods, mix ideas, or do something no one else has tried. This open-mindedness helps explain how simple questions can lead to amazing inventions and achievements.
Of course, curiosity and creativity are just part of the story. Turning a good idea into a real skill also takes learning, and the human brain is great at adapting. Even as adults, our brains can change and grow when we have new experiences. This is called neuroplasticity .
These changes can affect gray matter, which has many of the nerve cells that help the brain process information. Learning a tough skill makes the brain adjust to new tasks, and doing something over and over can change the parts of the brain involved.

items.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
items.desc: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.
items.text:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding , external
The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).

items.title: Mass badger cull ruled out by Welsh government after speculation
items.desc: Plaid Cymru ministers rule out mass badger cull as part of new plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis.
items.text:
Between 2013 and 2026, almost 250,000 badgers were killed in England as part of widespread culling to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB)
Plaid Cymru ministers have ruled out a mass badger cull as part of updated plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB).
It follows months of speculation over the Welsh government's intentions, after an expert group warned "a step change" was needed in efforts to eradicate the disease.
While farming leaders have long called for tougher badger controls, a petition against culling has attracted more than 28,000 signatures on the Senedd website in recent weeks.
The Welsh government said it would take "a new and pragmatic approach to TB eradication that is evidence-based and science-led".
While there will be no widespread cull, targeted measures are under consideration which could involve trapping and killing some badgers if they test positive for the disease.
But further research is needed first and no timetable has been set out.
Farming unions called for swifter action, while wildlife groups warned that killing badgers was "not off the table".
Reform calls for badger cull in fight against bovine TB
Young farmer in tears after TB hits 55 cows
Latest figures show nearly 96% of cattle herds in Wales are now TB free.
But the problem - which can be devastating for affected farms - is concentrated, with higher incidence levels in west Wales and along the border with England.
There were 10,090 cows slaughtered following TB testing in the 12 months to June 2026.
Under the previous Labour-run Welsh government, a target was set for Wales to completely eradicate bovine TB by 2041.
But before May's Senedd election an expert group set up to advise ministers , external warned that goal would "not be met", and called for urgent action and more funding.
Cattle are slaughtered if they are found to be carriers of bovine TB
The Bovine TB Eradication Programme Board's latest recommendations were published on Tuesday, alongside the government's response.
On badgers, ministers said they were "not pursuing a mass, non-selective cull".
However further research is proposed of the role played by badgers and deer in spreading the disease via new population surveys and fieldwork.
This would then lead to developing "targeted and proportionate" interventions which could include trapping and testing badgers before vaccinating or euthanising them, "where the evidence supports this".

items.title: 'Urgent action' needed to protect lake
items.desc: Tourism and outdated septic tanks are said to be adding to the ecological decline of Buttermere.
items.text:
Buttermere has been described as a "fragile ecosystem under pressure"
Tourism, infrastructure challenges and "outdated, undersized and poorly maintained" wastewater systems are contributing to the ecological decline of a popular lake, an environmental group has warned.
Buttermere, in the Lake District, has seen rising nutrient levels in recent years which can lead to excess phosphorus and blankets of algae.
A new report has found farming practices alone "cannot account" for the changes.
West Cumbria Rivers Trust (WCRT), a charity which tracked down the sources of phosphorus for the study, argues "urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed".
The Buttermere Nutrient Investigations Project was commissioned and funded by the Environment Agency (EA) after the lake was last year found to be failing to meet total phosphorus targets.
WCRT said the investigation showed Buttermere - a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest and Special Area of Conservation - was a "fragile ecosystem under pressure".
Buttermere is a naturally nutrient-poor lake, the organisation said, which provides a welcoming environment for sensitive species, such as the Arctic charr cold-water fish.
But algae triggered by excess phosphorus can "choke out these rare habitats and degrade the lake's protected status", WCRT added.
Local wastewater infrastructure was identified as a "key area of concern", the organisation said, while agricultural investigations across major landholdings found no evidence of systemic diffuse pollution or excessive nutrient use, with soil management plans broadly appropriate.
As they are not connected to mains drainage, many properties in the area rely on septic tanks or package treatment plants.
However, WCRT said a number of the 11 septic tank systems identified in the catchment were "undersized, poorly maintained or past their effective lifespan, with several suspected to be discharging directly to surface water, which is not compliant with the regulations".
Although most owners were keen to help the environment, the trust said there was a "widespread lack of awareness" about how the private systems worked and what level of maintenance was needed.
Surveys also revealed just over 40% of visitors had dogs with them and many were walked along sensitive lakeshore paths.
Nutrient fertilisation by the animals "could be significant", it was found.

items.text:
JoyDrops champions awards-eligible documentary shorts about joy, a counterweight to a category often dominated by tragedy. Good News Network has partnered with JoyDrops to spotlight these films and talk with the filmmakers behind them.
“Believe me, it never gets old,” Freddie Nole told GNN. “I’m serious.”
Nole is talking about the moment he meets a man walking out of prison, often someone with no one else coming to get him. He and his wife, Sue, take the man to a meal, buy him clothes, get him a phone and drive him to wherever he’s headed next. No two pickups are the same, he said, but one thing always is.
“The appreciation that these individuals express to us for just being there,” Nole said, “at a time when they’re most vulnerable.”
That work is at the heart of The Second Life of Freddie Nole , the latest film in GNN’s JoyDrops series.
Directed by Dana Nachman, the film rides along with Nole for a single day as he picks up a man leaving prison in Pennsylvania. Along the way, viewers learn that Nole knows this road personally. His full backstory comes only at the end.
Nachman, whose company, Sweet World Films, focuses on stories about repairing the world, had worked on wrongful conviction cases for years. But reentry was new to her. She and her business partner, Chelsea Matter, had a little money left over from another project and wanted a story that truly fit a short. A one-day road trip was the perfect container.
They reached out to Nole over Zoom. “Literally maybe 30 seconds of talking, I was like, oh God, this guy is special,” Nachman told GNN. “We call him movie gold. Freddie is life gold.”
She later learned that groups across the country do similar work, some just 50 miles from her home in Northern California. She’s glad she didn’t know sooner. “My ignorance got me to him, really,” she said.
Nole went to prison in 1969, when Richard Nixon was president. When he finally walked out, the only person he could count on was his wife, who had stood by him for more than 37 years.
He had sent her his clothing sizes so he wouldn’t stand out. They didn’t fit. “It was just a whole embarrassing situation for me,” he told GNN, “not so much the people, but that I was so detached from this normal society.”
Then he learned he was already in violation of his parole for not reporting in time. He spent four hours of his first night of freedom at the parole office. “My whole first day of being out was simply walking on pins and needles,” he said.

items.title: Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week
items.desc: Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week Design Miami, one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, an
items.text:
Brodin, “Constellation of Memory,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Kelley and Gavin Brodin.)
Design Miami , one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.
The theme, Unveiling , calls for the viewers to truly observe each object, deciphering what inspired the artist to create them, and the surrounding stories behind their choices. These may be hiding in plain sight or several times removed from the final result, reflecting something deeply personal or rooted in the artist’s culture. Unveiling is then divided among four curatorial threads, each with different approaches and best represented by certain artists, techniques, and galleries.
Pippin Drysdale, “Sacred Lands,” 2026. Adrian Sassoon at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Adrian Sassoon, London; photography by Robert Frith, Acorn Photo.)
First up is Process as Aesthetic: Unveiling the Hand of the Maker . This theme highlights the creative process, particularly the techniques, labor, and experimentation that come to determine an object’s aesthetic, regarding these steps as a vehicle for expression. This can be seen in the ceramic works of Bouke de Vries and Pippin Drysdale; Caroline Desile’s architecture-influenced Totem 1 ; Richard Haining’s STACKED creations, made up of thousands of pieces of salvaged New York City wood; and Man Ray’s Optic-Topic mask , the centerpiece of this division.
Le Corbusier, “La licorne passe sur la mer,” 1959. Boccara Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Boccara Gallery.)
Meanwhile, Subverting Archetypes: The Familiar, Reimagined , takes a more surrealist route, blurring the line between the familiar and the uncanny, asking viewers to reassess to what they think they know. Such is the case of a selection of 20th-century tapestries by Le Corbusier, Sonia Delaunay, and Alexander Calder. This section also features the work of Brazilian designer Lucas Recchia, who blends metal with fused glass, and a wall piece by Jaydan Moore, who turns found, silver-plated tableware into sculptural forms.
Dee Clements, “Gams,” 2026. Mindy Solomon Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: Clare Britt, courtesy of the artist and Mindy Solomon Gallery)
